newsitem.title: USA: FTC offers guidance on getting online data from kids.
newsitem.headline: FTC offers guidance on getting online data from kids.

text.p: Regulators Wednesday said it is against the law for online marketers to collect personal information from children in cyberspace without fully disclosing to a child's parent how the data will be used.

Responding to privacy concerns, the Federal Trade Commission gave online marketers guidance on how to avoid breaking the law when gathering names, e-mail addresses, phone numbers and other "personally identifiable information" from kids.

The agency said companies that operate Internet Web sites where such information is gathered must obtain parental consent before releasing the data to a third party, such as a company that could use the information to market products.

"Today's actions makes it clear that many of the practices currently used by online marketers to elicit personal information from children can be prosecuted by the FTC," said Kathryn Montgomery of the Centre for Media Education, or CME.

The advocacy group had charged in a report last year that advertisers and marketers were exploiting kids by pitching products in cyberspace in ways that manipulated children and violated their privacy.

In particular, CME said marketers peddling children's products were using a variety of techniques on computer online services and over the Internet to collect detailed data and compile individual profiles on kids.
The FTC made its position known in a public letter from its staff.
The letter was released after the agency had probed an Internet Web site for children aged 4-15 named "KidsCom." It is operated by a Milwaukee-based firm called Spectracom Inc.
According to the letter, KidsCom "represented that the information collection would enable the children to earn premiums, but did not also disclose the marketing uses of this information."
The FTC staff, however, recommended that the agency take no legal action after the KidsCome site was changed to address regulators' concerns.
